Snow Predictions for February 2025 East Coast USA

Major Storm Systems Expected

A powerful storm is forecasted to move from the South to the East starting in early February. This system could bring heavy snow, sleet, and freezing rain from the Central Plains to the Northeast. The possibility of a nor’easter forming by mid-month increases the risk of strong winds and heavy snowfall along the Eastern Seaboard.

A separate system is expected to develop later in the month, affecting states from Virginia to Maine. Meteorologists warn of potential ice accumulation, leading to dangerous road conditions and power outages. The Great Lakes region may also experience lake-effect snow, adding to overall precipitation totals.

title: Pittsburgh Winter Forecast 2026-2027: Snow & El Nino Outlook
contentHtml:
If you're trying to figure out what kind of winter Pittsburgh is in for during 2026-2027, there's one signal doing most of the talking this year: El Niño. It's already developed, it's expected to strengthen heading into winter, and it has a fairly predictable effect on this part of the country. That doesn't mean anyone can hand you a snowfall total for December, nobody honestly can, but it does shift the odds in a direction we can talk about. Here's what the science actually says, what it tends to mean for Pittsburgh, and how to get ready.

The big driver this year: a strengthening El Niño

Let's start with the one thing forecasters agree on. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center says El Niño conditions are present and are expected to strengthen through the winter of 2026-2027. The odds of it sticking around sit up near 97 to 99 percent. That's about as confident as seasonal forecasting gets. So what is it? El Niño is a warming of the tropical Pacific. It matters to us in Pennsylvania because it nudges the jet stream, the high-altitude air current that steers storms. Shift that path, and you shift where the cold and the snow land.

What El Niño usually means for Pittsburgh

Here's the part people don't always want to hear. In a typical El Niño winter, the northern tier of the country, Pittsburgh included, tends to run milder than average, with the main storm track pushed further south. In plain terms, that usually leans toward a warmer winter and near-to-below-normal snowfall for our area. The big, persistent Arctic outbreaks are generally less likely to set up shop for weeks at a time.

But, and this is a real but, "milder on average" is not the same as "no snow." El Niño also fires up the southern storm track, and every so often one of those systems rides up the coast or clips the region and dumps a heavy, wet snow in a single go. So the realistic picture is a winter that leans mild and quieter than usual, punctuated by the odd big storm that can still throw the seasonal average right back to normal. One well-placed system does a lot.

Pittsburgh's normal winter, for context

It helps to know the baseline. In a normal year, Pittsburgh picks up somewhere around 40 to 45 inches of snow across the season. Spread out, mostly, rather than dumped all at once. January is the coldest stretch. Highs often sit in the mid-30s, with nights below freezing. Lake-effect snow off Lake Erie occasionally reaches the northern suburbs, though the city sits far enough south to dodge the worst of what places like Erie get. If the coming winter lands below that 40-inch mark, that would be a fairly textbook El Niño outcome.

What the almanacs say

Plenty of people still swing by the Farmers' Almanac and the Old Farmer's Almanac for a winter read, so it's worth being straight about them. As of mid-2026, the Old Farmer's Almanac has confirmed that El Niño is the headline signal it's watching, but its full, month-by-month regional forecast for 2026-2027 lands in the 2027 edition, which wasn't fully out yet at the time of writing. Worth remembering too: these almanacs use their own long-range methods, and even meteorologists treat their specific predictions with a healthy dose of caution. Read them for fun, lean on NOAA's outlooks for the science.

So how much snow will Pittsburgh get in 2026-2027?

The honest answer? No one can give you a firm number in advance. Anyone who does is guessing. What the evidence supports is a lean, not a lock. A milder-than-average winter with near-to-below-normal snowfall looks more likely than a brutal, snowy one, thanks to El Niño. Just don't sell the shovel on the strength of that. Seasonal outlooks deal in probabilities, and a single storm can rewrite the story in a day. Treat it as "prepare for a normal winter, but don't be shocked if it's on the quieter side."

How to prepare, either way

Whatever the season throws at you, the prep is the same, and it's cheap insurance.

  • Get the car winter-ready: check tyres, battery, wipers and antifreeze before the first cold snap.
  • Keep a basic kit in the boot, a scraper, a small shovel, a blanket and some salt or grit.
  • Stock a few days of essentials at home in case a storm knocks out power or makes the roads a mess.
  • Follow the National Weather Service and local forecasts for the short-range detail, which is far more reliable a few days out than any seasonal outlook.

Frequently asked questions

Will Pittsburgh have a snowy winter in 2026-2027?

Current signals lean toward a milder winter with near-to-below-normal snowfall, because a strengthening El Niño typically pushes the main storm track south of our region. That said, it is a lean, not a guarantee, and a single well-placed storm can still bring heavy snow.

What is causing the 2026-2027 winter pattern?

El Niño, a warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center expects it to be present and strengthening through the winter, with very high confidence. El Niño shifts the jet stream, which changes where cold air and storms are most likely to track.

How much snow does Pittsburgh usually get?

In a normal season, Pittsburgh receives roughly 40 to 45 inches of snow, with January typically the coldest month. A below-average total this winter would be a fairly typical El Niño result, though averages can be skewed by one or two big storms.

Can I trust the Farmers' Almanac winter forecast?

Treat it as entertainment more than science. The almanacs use their own long-range methods, and their detailed 2026-2027 regional forecast appears in the 2027 edition. For the most reliable guidance, rely on NOAA's seasonal outlooks and short-range National Weather Service forecasts.

When is Pittsburgh's coldest and snowiest period?

Typically January into early February, when temperatures are lowest and the snow is most persistent. December and late February can also bring significant snow, but the deepest cold usually settles in around mid-winter.

The winter weather forecast for Europe in 2024/2025 is complex and subject to change, but here’s what we know so far:

Temperature: Overall, a warmer winter is expected for much of the continent. This is due to the influence of a high-pressure system extending across Europe. However some northern parts might experience colder temperatures under the jet stream.
Precipitation: A drier season is predicted for most of Europe due to the high-pressure system. However, the north and southeast might see more precipitation than normal.

Snowfall : The seasonal outlook predicts below-average snowfall for most of the continent. However, Scandinavia is expected to experience increased snowfall, influenced by a dominant low-pressure system and a shifting jet stream.

Overall: AccuWeather predicts a colder-than-normal winter for much of Europe, with increased chances of snowfall and colder temperatures compared to recent years.

Specific Regions:

Northern Europe: Significant snowfall is expected in the Nordic countries, especially Scandinavia, with colder-than-normal temperatures.
Central Europe: A mix of wintry weather is forecast, with periods of snowfall, freezing temperatures, and occasional milder spells.
Southern Europe: While temperatures will be milder compared to the north, some regions may experience colder-than-normal conditions, especially in the mountains.

Old Farmer’s Almanac:

Overall: The Old Farmer’s Almanac predicts a winter with below-average temperatures for much of Europe.

Specific Regions:

  • Northern Europe: Cold, snowy conditions are expected, with frequent winter storms.
  • Central Europe: A mix of snow and rain is forecast, with occasional cold spells.
  • Southern Europe: Milder temperatures are predicted, although some regions may experience occasional cold snaps.

NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration):

Overall: NOAA’s long-range forecast suggests a winter with near-normal temperatures for most of Europe.

Specific Regions:

  • Northern Europe: A mix of cold and mild conditions is expected, with occasional snowfall.
  • Central Europe: Temperatures are likely to fluctuate, with periods of cold and mild weather.
  • Southern Europe: Milder-than-normal temperatures are predicted, with occasional rain and snow in the mountains.

OnTheSnow:

Overall: OnTheSnow focuses on winter sports enthusiasts and predicts a good winter for skiing and snowboarding in many European resorts.

Specific Regions:

  • Alps: Significant snowfall is expected in the Alps, providing excellent conditions for winter sports.
  • Pyrenees: Good snowfall is also forecast for the Pyrenees, making it a great destination for winter sports.
  • Scandinavia: Abundant snowfall is predicted, offering excellent opportunities for skiing and snowboarding.

Weather in Europe in january 2025

January in Europe is typically a cold month, especially in the northern and eastern parts. However, the weather can vary significantly depending on the specific region. Here’s a general overview:

Northern and Eastern Europe:

  • Temperatures: Cold, often below freezing.
  • Snowfall: Frequent snowfall, especially in mountainous areas.
  • Daylight: Short days with limited sunlight.

Central Europe:

  • Temperatures: Cold to mild, with occasional freezing temperatures.
  • Snowfall: Possible snowfall, especially in higher altitudes.
  • Daylight: Moderate daylight hours.

Southern Europe:

  • Temperatures: Mild, with occasional cold spells.
  • Snowfall: Uncommon, except in mountainous regions.
  • Daylight: Longer days with more sunlight.

What will winter be like in Indiana?

Indiana can expect a cold, snowy, and wet winter season, with several snow events and cold snaps throughout. Expect typical Midwestern winter conditions, with more frequent precipitation and colder-than-average temperatures.

Texas will see a varied winter. Northern Texas may experience more extreme cold, while other areas will have milder temperatures mixed with rainy spells. Winter will be milder in some regions but cold snaps are likely in the north.

Tennessee’s winter is expected to be colder than usual, with a mix of rain, snow, and ice possible at different points. Prepare for fluctuating conditions, with a few significant cold spells and precipitation events.

Minnesota will likely see colder-than-average temperatures, but not as extreme as in previous years. Snowfall is predicted to be slightly below average, with the heaviest snow expected in late November, December, January, and early February.
